newsitem.title: JAPAN: US sailor gets 13 yrs for slashing Japanese woman.
newsitem.headline: US sailor gets 13 yrs for slashing Japanese woman.

text.p: A Japanese court on Wednesday sentenced a U.S. sailor to 13 years in prison for slashing a woman's throat as he robbed her in a port near Nagasaki.

Seaman First-Class Terrence Michael Swanson attacked the woman with a knife in the port of Sasebo, southern Japan, where he was serving on the missile frigate U.S.S. McLusky. He robbed her of 13,000 yen ($115).
Swanson, 20, from Anoka, Minnesota, was arrested four days after the July 16 attack and pleaded guilty in September to attempted murder and robbery.
The woman, also 20, suffered severe injuries and spent 26 days in hospital followed by five months of rehabilitation, an official of Nagasaki District Court said.

"Even though he (Swanson) was fully aware he could kill her, he slashed the victim's throat without hesitation. This was an extremely brutal, evil deed for which there are no mitigating circumstances," Judge Kiyomi Yano said in passing sentence at Nagasaki District Court.

The U.S. Navy said in August it had paid compensation of $25,000 to the woman and the commander of U.S. naval forces at Sasebo, 920 km (570 miles) south of Tokyo, apologised to the governor of Nagasaki Prefecture.

It is the first such conviction since the two governments signed an agreement last year streamlining procedures under which Japanese authorities can deal with crimes by U.S. military personnel stationed in Japan, the official said.

The agreement, which gives Japanese authorities prompt access to U.S. military suspects, was reached after the rape of a 12-year-old schoolgirl by three U.S. servicemen on the southern Japanese island of Okinawa in September of last year.
The three servicemen were jailed for up to 10 years.

Violent crimes by members of the 47,000-strong U.S. forces stationed in Japan have caused an outcry against the U.S. military presence, which both Tokyo and Washington say is necessary to maintain regional security and stability.

On Monday, U.S. and Japanese officials concluded a year of negotiations on the bases with an agreement to cut the U.S. presence on Okinawa and a plan for a revolutionary floating helicopter base off the island. ($1=113 yen)
